title: Christopher Doyle's works outside WKW Collaborations

commenti.body: [removed]
Outside of his Wong Kar-Wai films I think you definitely have to check out Zhang Yimou’s Hero from 2002. I think it’s Doyle’s best work and one of the best looking movies of all time in general.

He has had an astonishingly broad patchwork of fruitful collaborations. From Taiwanese and Hong Kong new wave (including WKW), to sweeping Chinese epics (Chen Kaige + Zhang Yimou), to American auteurs (Gus Van Sant, Jon Favreaux, Jim Jarmusch), to established independent English, Irish, Japanese and Australian filmmakers. He seems to bring a wild-card infusion of exoticism and an utterly unique chameleon-like aesthetic that somehow conforms to the framing of, say, a James Ivory, or an M. Night Shyamalan film, and yet retains some kind of crackling otherworldly experimental flair that - however muted - always keeps me completely under his spell. 

I loved the saturated stillness of Philip Noyce’s Rabbit Proof Fence, the unconventional framing in buddy comedy Made, his frames within frames, lens and angle choices and sculptural orphaned body parts in Pen-Ek Ratanaruang’s Invisible Waves, the surrealist Boschian carnavalia of Jodorowsky’s Endless Poetry… he’s a DOP that world class DOPs hire to shoot films that they direct (Gu Changwei’s Love for Life). 

He is equally at home in period drama as horror, as magic realism, as threadbare indie. All that would be impressive enough even if he had never worked with Wong Kar Wai, but once you add those films to the mix, that elevates him - in my very humble, clearly biased opinion - to one of the greatest to do it.

One that sticks out for me is The Limits of Control by Jim Jarmusch. Unlike Paterson (a complete masterpiece), I really don't care very much for the film (it just ends up feeling like arthouse self-parody with a lot of its obfuscation and quirks), but Doyle's cinematography of the Spanish environments is absolutely stunning, and there's also a wonderful flamenco guitar playing sequence.

The first feature he directed, *Away with Words*, is a wild ride and well worth tracking down. I wish it was more readily available, and in better quality - even the couple of legit DVD releases it got already looked rough by the standards of the era, and it's been MIA since (there hasn't been a legal way to watch or buy it since 2009).

It's gorgeous from beginning to end, totally bonkers, and just overflowing with creative energy. It's not long but it can actually get wearying if you're not on its wavelength.

I've watched it four or five times over the years and there are 100 stunning images from it that are etched on my brain forever, but I can't remember the first thing about how any of them fit together. Which is probably what he was going for, to be honest (it's right there in the title: away with words, i.e. away with story structure that has any literary basis).

Not a film, but the Hong Kong episode he shot for Bourdain's Parts Unknown captured than the city better than most local movies do.

Plus, it was the last episode filmed before Bourdain died, and the last true depiction of the city before it felt into protests and the National Security Law was enacted. So it's pretty momentous for Hongkongers, especially as Doyle was heavily involved.

I agree. It’s easily my least favourite Jarmusch movie, but boy does it look good. I remember watching a little making-of featurette, where Jarmusch was just wandering around getting lost in the town, and it would cut back to Doyle running around set, working harder than anyone.

*Last Life in the Universe (2003)* ..it's not exactly similar to WKW's films, but, is great, in it's own way.. IDK how to describe the cinematography but from my memory the style felt different from what we usually see in WKW films. It was beautiful. I remember replaying several scenes because of just how beautiful they were... my saying this makes no sense haha, but it was a really beautiful film on all levels.. it's like a little home in itself.
I watched [Love After Love](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt10415576/?ref_=nm_flmg_t_3_cin) and it was beautiful, not a stellar story but I was so sunk into the visuals it didn't matter:)
That’s hardly surprising to hear when you watch the movie since it seems so relaxed but the cinematography is incredibly focused, haha.
Absolutely love this film. On our first date, my now husband and I talked about this and I'd never met anyone else who had seen it.
